speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: asked the Minister for Transport in view of the high Certificate of Entitlement (COE) Category C prices, whether the Ministry can consider providing additional support to SMEs with a turnover of less than S$100 million that need to extend the COEs of their commercial vehicles in order to continue their trade.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) with the prices of Certificates of Entitlement showing no sign of abating, what is the anticipated impact on the current inflationary situation, especially in sectors reliant on vehicular transport; and (b) whether there are specific measures in the pipeline to mitigate such impact on sectors heavily reliant on transport for deliveries like food and groceries.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: asked the Minister for Transport whether he can consider providing additional support to existing owners of commercial vehicles who require these vehicles to continue their trade in light of high COE Category C prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) what is the total number of cars currently available for car sharing; and (b) whether the Ministry will consider increasing the allocation of cars for car sharing and exclude these from the bidding for Certificates of Entitlement to make car sharing an attractive option for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) whether the Government has data on the current percentage of cars in Singapore that are of shared car fleets, excluding taxis and private hire vehicles; and (b) if so, how much have such fleets grown in the past five years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) in view of the position taken for commercial vehicles' growth and the significantly smaller road footprint of motorcycles in general, whether the Ministry has conducted any studies allowing for a marginal growth in the number of motorcycles on Singapore's road space management; and (b) if not, why not.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for Transport in view of the increases in private hire car population and demand for such services, whether the Ministry will consider (i) mandating the number of hours that private hire vehicles must be on the roads to serve its purpose and (ii) tightening the conditions which enable personal cars to be converted for commercial usage, such as setting a limit on Category A COEs allowed for this conversion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: My residents and stallholders have also shared their feedback with me during my market and house visits.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, I will recap why our zero-vehicle growth policy remains relevant, as the COE system is one of the policy measures, which supports this goal.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, I will clarify some of the questions that Members in this House and the public have raised regarding how the COE system operates.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is not tenable for our vehicle population to keep increasing, as it means that we have to either set aside more land to build more roads, or accept higher levels of congestion like what we see in many overseas cities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government's aim is to build an accessible, inclusive and sustainable land transport system that meets the needs of all Singaporeans, while bearing in mind our two key constraints: land and carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Reflecting the views of many Singaporeans, we have adopted a "car-lite" strategy and placed mass public transport at the core of our transport strategy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Currently, 64% of peak-period journeys are made on public transport and we aim to increase this to 75% by 2030 as we expand our Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) network.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Conversely, the percentage of car-owning resident households has fallen from 40% in 2013 to about one-third in recent years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mass public transport enables the greatest number of people to get to their destinations with the least land take and carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With our current energy mix where the bulk of our electricity is generated using natural gas, a journey that is made on an electric vehicle emits 50% of the carbon compared to an internal combustion engine vehicle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, if the journey is made using an electric bus, the carbon emission level drops to 30%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Using MRT is even better, as the carbon emission level is only 10% compared to an internal combustion engine vehicle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are also expanding our public transport network significantly – an additional 100 kilometres of rail by 2035, which is almost 40% increase from our current network.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Today, seven in 10 households are within a 10-minute walk of one of our 202 MRT and Light Rapid Transit (LRT) stations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: By the next decade, it will be eight in 10 households.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Besides mass public transport, we are also enhancing the first-and-last-mile options such as walking and cycling, as well as access to point-to-point (P2P) services offered by taxis, private hire vehicles and car-sharing vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These provide options for Singaporeans who do not own cars, but may need to use cars as a service from time to time, for example to take family outings during weekends or to send their parents for medical appointments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Members are aware, the COE system is an allocation mechanism for our vehicle quota, to achieve the zero-vehicle growth policy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: COE bidding takes place twice a month and the bid prices can fluctuate depending on the prevailing demand and supply.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When demand is weaker and there is plentiful supply, prices will be lower.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, when supply is tight, like what we are experiencing for the past year, and demand is strong, prices will increase.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Over the last three quarters, or from February 2023 to October 2023, the largest driver of demand has been from Singapore residents.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Three in four Category A (Cat A) COEs and two in three Cat B COEs were won by Singapore residents.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In comparison, foreigners won 1% of Cat A COEs and 4% of Cat B COEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is clear that the increase in COE prices was not due to foreign buyers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some have asked if the high COE prices were caused by households who own multiple cars and whether we should impose additional taxes on such households when they purchase their second or subsequent vehicle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The percentage of multiple car-owning households has been reducing – from about 19% of car-owning households in 2012 to less than 15% today.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This translates to just 5% of all households in Singapore, since about one-third of households own cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Given the low proportion, demand-measures such as imposing additional taxes on foreigners or households that own multiple cars would have little effect on COE prices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These companies won about 21% of Cat A COEs in the last three quarters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is lower than the 27% of Cat A COEs they won in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, in the most recent bidding exercise, car-leasing companies won only 16% of the Cat A quota.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Their proportion of Cat B winning bids also reduced slightly from 24% in 2022 to 23% in the last three quarters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The data shows that COE prices have gone up in a period where demand from car-leasing companies has come down, so it is unlikely that they are the main factor for the increase in COE prices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are two categories of PHCs: self-drive PHCs and chauffeured PHCs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Both are available for rentals, but only chauffeured PHCs may be used to provide ride-hail services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As of September 2023, the total PHC population is around 78,000 – similar to what it was in end-2019.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: About two-thirds are chauffeured PHCs and the remaining are self-drive PHCs including car-sharing vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Two-thirds of PDVL holders who made at least one ride-hail trip in September 2023 drive company-owned cars, while the rest drive cars owned by individuals, including their own vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The demand for P2P services is increasingly met by PHCs rather than taxis.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Pre-COVID, PHCs provided around three out of every five P2P trips.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This has increased to about two out of every three P2P trips as of September 2023.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: PHCs therefore play an important role in ensuring the availability of P2P services for commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They also serve more individuals and households compared to private cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In addition, PHCs allow our drivers to earn a living using their own cars or leasing from PHC companies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested having a separate COE category for car-leasing companies or treat them like taxis which do not have to bid for COEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are trade-offs to having a separate COE category for car-leasing companies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Similar to taxis, the quota for this new category would have to be drawn from existing categories given our zero-growth policy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As PHC demand is still evolving and could vary from quarter to quarter, it is difficult to ascertain what is the exact quota required to meet the needs of drivers and commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we move too much of the existing quota from Cat A and B to this new category for PHC companies, it will further reduce the supply in these categories and there is a risk that COE prices may spike further.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the other hand, if we do not move enough quota to the new category, drivers will end up with insufficient vehicles to rent and commuters could be affected by shortages in P2P services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will study if there are further options beyond COE bidding to address the concerns with car-leasing companies, recognising that PHCs do travel longer distances on our roads but they also serve an important function in providing P2P services for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Next, let me turn to concerns over speculative demand, including by dealers, as raised by Mr Saktiandi Supaat.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have a suite of measures in place to discourage speculation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For Cat A and B, there are a number of restrictions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Temporary COE (TCOE) bid must be made in the name of the buyer and transfers are not allowed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For Cat E, the validity period of the TCOE is shorter, at three months.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Specifically for Cat E, we have seen that the TCOEs are used to register vehicles, on average, within 14 days, way before the validity period of three months.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Since January 2023, only one Cat E TCOE has expired.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This shows that the dealers are not speculating, but are bidding based on actual demand.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The large majority of bids for cars are clustered within a small range around the clearing price, with most bids being made within the final hour of bidding.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This shows that bidders are closely monitoring the clearing price and making bids based on their willingness to pay, while not paying more than necessary.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is typically not in the interests of dealers to bid higher than what is necessary to win the bid, as they have to absorb the higher COE prices since they have committed to certain sale prices for their vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to closely monitor the COE market to detect speculative behaviour and, if necessary, we will introduce further measures to discourage such behaviour.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government will also take enforcement action against dealers who make false claims or misleading representations to consumers on the nature of their transactions, for example, if they claim that consumers would have ownership of the motor vehicle with a 100% loan with no down payment when, in effect, consumers are merely leasing it from them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Under a zero-growth policy, the number of COEs available for bidding is based on the number of deregistered vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For Cat A, B and C, we are currently facing a tight supply situation because many of the existing vehicles have not reached the end of their COE period and are not due for deregistration.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Large differences in the supply during the peak and trough years result in higher volatility in COE prices across different years, assuming demand stays relatively constant.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: A better outcome can be achieved for all stakeholders, while still allowing the COE system to play its role as an allocation mechanism, if we can reduce the peak-to-trough ratio, by using a "cut-and-fill" approach to shave off the future peaks and using the supply to fill the current troughs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have previously made several moves to reduce volatility in quota supply.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Instead of just the preceding quarter, we now use the moving average of deregistrations in the four preceding quarters to compute COE quotas for the next quarter.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In May 2023, MOT announced that we will bring forward the quota from guaranteed deregistrations in the peak years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This has helped to increase COE supply over the last six months.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On a quarter-on-quarter basis, Cat A supply increased by 11% in the second quarter and then 22% in the third quarter this year, while Cat B supply increased by 3% and 6% in the second and third quarter of this year respectively.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, demand has remained very strong and COE prices have continued to rise.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will, therefore, do further cut-and-fill to bring forward more quota from the peak years to fill the current troughs, while maintaining our zero-vehicle growth policy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Industry players have welcomed this move, as the additional supply injection this time is more significant, compared what we have done in previous quarters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As one motor dealer representative commented to The Straits Times, "more COE quota will be made available going forward.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is no need to rush." With the increase in supply, we hope that COE prices would moderate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, we know prices will also depend on market demand, and demand is not within the Government's control.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I need to be upfront with everyone that it is not possible to predict how prices will move in the next few rounds of COE bidding, but I want to assure hon Members and the public that the Ministry of Transport (MOT) and the Land Transport Authority (LTA) are doing what we can to address the concerns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to closely monitor and explore ideas to improve the situation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, Mr Don Wee, Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about this segment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Like Cat A and B, the quota supply for Cat C has also been rising in the recent quarters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It rose 58% in the second quarter and 66% in the third quarter.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This has helped to moderate the Cat C prices, which have largely kept within the S$80,000 to S$85,000 range in the last few quarters, coming down from more than S$91,000 in March this year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about allowing a marginal growth in the number of motorcycles, given our approach for commercial vehicles and in view that motorcycles take up less road space.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Murali Pillai had raised a similar suggestion in this House in November last year and MOT had explained that we have no plans to increase the growth rate of motorcycles as part of our zero-growth policy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is true that motorcycles have a smaller footprint on the roads than cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, they can still contribute to congestion, as what we can see from the experiences of other cities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As individuals who own motorcycles may use them for both commercial and personal purposes, such use of motorcycles is similar to private hire cars, as compared to commercial vehicles which are used predominantly for business needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The zero-growth rate policy, therefore, applies to both cars and motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That said, the Government recognises that some Singaporeans rely on motorcycles for their livelihoods and there are also higher proportions of lower-income individuals among motorcycle-owners, compared to car owners.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is one reason why the Additional Registration Fees (ARF), road taxes and Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) charges for motorcycles are lower, compared to other vehicle types.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To safeguard against speculative bidding behaviour for Cat D COE, MOT introduced several measures in the last two years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These include raising the Cat D TCOE bid deposit to S$1,500 and reducing the TCOE validity period to one month.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Cat D COE prices have come down from more than S$13,000 in November 2022 and have stayed at around S$11,000 in recent bidding exercises.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to study ways to improve the COE system for Cat D, including ideas which share the same intent as what Mr Singh and Mr Murali have raised.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With regard to the "cut-and-fill" approach, will there be any trade-offs in respect of the impact on the roads with this initial reduction of the peaks and troughs that the Senior Minister of State mentioned?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second clarification is that I am glad to hear that LTA is looking at the COE market, in terms of speculative activities in relation to my Parliamentary Question, and I am wondering whether the Senior Minister of State can share a bit more about the possibilities on what are the measures that we can take to relook into the speculative activities going forward, on the side of car COEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And the trade-off is this: because when we do "cut-and-fill", we are effectively borrowing from the future.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are taking the supply in the future peak years and we "cut" this to "fill" the current troughs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we are borrowing from the future peak years, ahead of time, before these cars are actually deregistered.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But this is a trade-off that we have to make in order to strike a balance between the volatility and to be able to do some "cut and fill" to raise the supply in the current trough years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And that is also why, because of this trade-off, we have to be quite calibrated and not overdo this "cut-and-fill", because there will be downsides in the short term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, given the recent rise in the COE prices, we are concerned about whether the average Singaporeans will be squeezed out of car-owning opportunities very fast in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result of that, I would like to raise two supplementary questions to the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, do not look at the 1,614 in isolation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Please add up also what we had earlier injected and look at the complete picture.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The second supplementary question that Mr Leong raised, the design of our system is that we have the different categories contributing to Cat E, the Open category, and then the people who bid for Cat E can then decide what cars they want to use it for.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we look at Cat C, which is a question that Mr Leong has filed, because we have a growth rate of 0.25%, it is not zero-growth for Cat C.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, what happens is that the number of COEs that we transfer out of Cat C is still less than the number of new COEs that we have injected.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the overall supply for Cat C has continued to rise, albeit less than if we have not taken out to transfer to Cat E.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the overall supply for Cat C has been increasing over the years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to monitor the situation carefully.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And what we have done recently, with the additional injections into for Cat C, I hope it will help our business owners.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, will the high COE lead to fewer cars deregistering?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, is there an increasing trend or decreasing trend for high-end cars purchased as a result of higher ARF that has been introduced?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, are there any plans to change it to a usage-based system, that is to say, drivers will be charged based on usage?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Maybe what Mr Gan meant was that they then extend their COEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is the individual's prerogative because, all along, we have allowed this option that if you extend your COE by five years, then you cannot extend anymore; but if you extend by 10 years, we allow you to extend.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But when we look at it from a systems point of view, we have to bear in mind that most people do not extend their cars because we have a policy as well that if you extend your cars beyond 10 years, the road tax that you have to pay will be higher.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, what we have found is that the large majority of car owners, whether in years when the COE prices are lower, also including when years when COE prices are higher, most people do not keep on extending.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And if you look at car ownership system as a whole, beyond COE, that is why we have the ARF tiered in a very progressive manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you buy a more mass market car, typically it will be in Cat A; and for most of the cars in Cat A, the amount of ARF you pay will be a lot less than if you were to buy a bigger car and, certainly, a lot less, than if you were to buy a luxury car.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Can I ask Mr Gan to repeat his last question?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As to whether we can look at the ERP policy, whether there is room to tweak this further?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the past, some people have suggested whether it is possible to tilt more towards usage and then, therefore, give us a bit more confidence on the car population side of the house.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are things that we can continue to review.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I do want to point out that there is a need for both tools.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because if you only rely on usage, it will not be adequate, it will not be enough; if you only rely on controlling the population, then you are also not achieving the optimal outcome.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think the best balance is to have both: control the car population, but also look at usage-based.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Speaker, many small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are facing manpower constraints and rising business costs which include the escalating COEs when they refresh their commercial vans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am enlightened by MOT's consideration, as explained by the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MOT work with agencies, like Enterprise Singapore and PUB, to promote the application of schemes like the Enterprise Sustainability Programme and Energy Efficient Grant so that the SMEs can reduce the overall business costs via these schemes?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are different ways of helping our SMEs to reduce costs and to look at how to increase also on the other side, that means, it is not just the cost side of the equation, but also to help them to be able to increase their revenue and improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Senior Minister of State as we incrementally increase our road spaces and more vehicles are converted to EVs, will there be scope to review these numbers to have some growth when capacity can take it?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, we need to recognise that we cannot keep on building roads.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is a cost to doing that because the roads will take up land.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, instead of building roads, if we could use the space that is taking up by roads for other purposes, it could generate more value for society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: One example I can share with Mr Liang and the House is that as part of the North-South corridor, because we are building this corridor and moving the cars underground and, therefore, freeing up some of the surface space.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, over the next few years as a project is being completed, we will go round and talk to different communities along this stretch of the North-South corridor to explore how we can make better use of the surface space that is freed up.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, instead of roads, we use it for gardens, community space, public spaces, cycling and walking.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is something which we need to bear in mind.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is a trade-off to building more roads to cater to more cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second is: are there better ways to allow our people to still meet their commuting needs without necessarily having to own a car?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is one option, of course, that will still be available to some Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But for the majority of households, which as I mentioned earlier, now only one-third of resident households own a car and two-thirds do not.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the main mode will be public transport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think what we can do to also meet their needs where on occasions they need the P2P service is to look at how we can also enhance point-to-point services and car-sharing services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I just have a very short supplementary question which relates to my Parliamentary Question No 38.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I would say it is not focused only on the COE issue, even though today we are here in this House talking about the COE issue right now.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But this P2P review is actually a larger review looking at how P2P services can better meet the evolving needs of commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we will share more information with the House when the study is completed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are now going through the different parts of it together with our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, that is what the statistics tell us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I just wish to ask the Senior Minister of State if the Ministry would consider redeploying some Cat B supply to Cat A, especially in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe that at least part of the demand for Cat B will not be fungible and, therefore, will not move to Cat A.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, net-net, I am asking if the Ministry would consider increasing Cat A supply, which should mean decreasing Cat B supply, but I believe for the benefit of a middle-income Singaporean household who may just need to own an entry-level car.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I think we need to be mindful of the trade-offs when we make such a move.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As we can see from the recent bids, there is a strong demand from Singaporean buyers for both Cat A and Cat B.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, in deciding how to re-allocate, we have to bear that in mind as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is actually the same kind of complexities that I explained earlier about why there are trade-offs to having a separate category for private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because then, how do you decide how much to shift, to re-allocate?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And if you do not do it correctly, it will actually lead to more negative outcomes for everyone.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I ask whether MOT has done a study into what percentage of motorcycles is being used for commercial purposes, compared to private cars?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second clarification is: does the Senior Minister of State have a breakdown of the percentage of COEs in the Open category that is eventually registered to the different categories?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And when these COEs are being used to register, say, for Cat B vehicles, when it is deregistered, does the COE go back to the Open category or does it go to the Cat B category?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our Light Goods Vehicles ARF is also set at a lower rate: 5% of open market value (OMV), which is much lower than cars as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we do recognise and we will, as part of the policy that we set, try and see how we can cushion and provide more help for these categories of vehicle owners, while not going against the fundamental principles that, ultimately, defines COE as an allocation mechanism, and we do need to allow the market to work to decide how to allocate the limited supply of COEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And in different cases, and for different individuals, the proportion may actually change.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some of them do use it for commercial purposes from time to time, some of them use it more frequently, similar for PHCs that are owned by individuals.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think it is very difficult for us to tell for sure that this is the exact percentage.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But what we recognise is that the nature of how these motorcycles are being used is similar to PHCs because you use it effectively for dual use, unlike say, commercial vehicles, where it is mainly, predominantly for business needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if the Open category bids are being won and it is being then used for a certain category, it actually reflects what the buyers, what the market demand is.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are different ways of addressing the need for a more progressive system.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I would put forth to Ms Poa and to the House that COE, while there is an element of that in having Cat A and B, it is actually not the only tool that we have to achieve that progressive element in our car ownership system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just one question for the Acting Minister for Transport.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government, or specifically LTA, determine at any given point what is the appropriate number of motorcycles on the road in view of the incomes of Singaporeans across the board?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the past, we have had situations where motorcycle COEs were transferred to Open category, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, how does the LTA determine and regulate what would be the appropriate level of motorcycle ownership in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, now it is not done for Cat D anymore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because the risk of doing that is it then becomes a structural change and then, every year you will have an increase.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And the downsides of road congestion that can be caused by motorcycles, even though they take up less road space, are still there.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we will study the intent of what Mr Singh and Mr Murali Pillai had raised earlier to see what steps we can take on motorcycle COEs.
